passages.happening:
Moses sets out what will follow if Israel listens. “Now if you faithfully obey the voice of the LORD your God and are careful to follow all His commandments I am giving you today, the LORD your God will set you high above all the nations of the earth” (verse 1).

The good things are named one after another. There will be good in the city and in the country. There will be children, crops and young animals. The basket and the kneading bowl will be full. There will be good on coming in and on going out (verses 3-6).

Enemies who attack ‘will march out against you in one direction but flee from you in seven’ (verse 7). God will open the heavens and send rain in its season (verse 12). “The LORD will make you the head and not the tail” (verse 13).

And at the center: “The LORD will establish you as His holy people, just as He has sworn to you” (verse 9). “Then all the peoples of the earth will see that you are called by the name of the LORD” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The treaties of the ancient world ended with blessings for loyalty and curses for betrayal. This chapter is that part of Israel's covenant.

The blessings cover the whole of an Israelite's life. City and country are where people live. The basket and the kneading bowl are each day's bread. ‘When you come in’ and ‘when you go out’ takes in every activity from morning to night. In a land without a great river, rain in its season meant life. To lend and not borrow, to be the head and not the tail, meant a nation that was free and not in debt to foreign powers.

In the Old Testament a blessing is more than a kind wish. It is God's own favor, which gives life and makes things grow.

Look at who is addressed. The blessings are promised to Israel as a nation, living in its land under this covenant. The ‘you’ is the people as a whole, over time. The chapter is not a promise that each faithful person will be rich and well.

The blessings also have a purpose beyond Israel. Verse 10 says that the peoples of the earth will see. A nation living well under God's law was meant to be seen by others. Moses said the same in chapter 4.

The word ‘if’ stands at the beginning, the middle and the end (verses 1, 9 and 13). And the passage closes with the warning that matters most in this book: ‘do not go after other gods to serve them’ (verse 14).
passages.later:
God's first words to Abraham were words of blessing with the nations in view: “and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3).

Jesus opened his best-known sermon with blessings, and gave them to people this chapter's list would not lead anyone to expect: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:3-4).

Paul says where the Christian's blessing is found: God ‘has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms’ (Ephesians 1:3).
passages.hard:
Does this passage promise health and wealth to anyone who obeys God?

No. The chapter promises blessing and curse to Israel as a covenant nation in its land. It does not promise that every faithful person will do well.

The rest of the Old Testament makes that clear. Job is righteous and suffers terribly, and God rebukes the friends who insisted that his suffering must be a punishment: “you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has” (Job 42:7). Psalm 73 struggles with the fact that the wicked do well. The book of Ecclesiastes observes that the righteous sometimes perish in their righteousness.

Christians have read the chapter in more than one way. Some stress that its blessings and curses belonged to Israel's national covenant under the law, and were worked out in Israel's history and in Christ. Others see in it lasting principles of how God deals with nations. What the Bible as a whole will not support is the teaching, sometimes called the prosperity gospel, that faith guarantees money and health. Jesus told his followers, “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:33).
passages.asks: Every blessing in this passage is something received: rain, children, harvest and safety. Ask what you have that you did not make, and whether you thank God for it. And ask whether you have ever measured God's love for you by how well your life is going.

passages.happening:
Then the other side. “If, however, you do not obey the LORD your God by carefully following all His commandments and statutes I am giving you today, all these curses will come upon you and overtake you” (verse 15).

The first curses turn the blessings upside down, almost word for word. The city and the country, the basket and the kneading bowl, the children and the herds, the coming in and the going out are named again, each under a curse (verses 16-19).

Then they build. There will be disease and fever, drought and blight (verses 21-22). “The sky over your head will be bronze, and the earth beneath you iron” (verse 23). There will be defeat in battle: ‘You will march out against them in one direction but flee from them in seven’ (verse 25). There will be confusion of mind, and loss after loss. A man will build a house and not live in it. He will plant a vineyard and not taste its fruit (verse 30). Sons and daughters will be given to another nation (verse 32). The king will be carried off to a foreign land (verse 36).

“All these curses will come upon you. They will pursue you and overtake you until you are destroyed, since you did not obey the LORD your God” (verse 45).
passages.hearers:
The curses take up fifty-four verses, and the blessings fourteen. The weight is deliberate. Moses expects that Israel will fail, and he says so in chapter 31.

A curse here is a blessing reversed. The chapter goes through the same parts of life, city and field, food, children, herds and rain, and takes each one away. In a farming land with no great river, a sky like bronze and ground like iron meant no rain and no harvest. The same picture is found in the treaty of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon from 672 BC.

The curses also undo Israel's story. The diseases of Egypt come back (verse 27). The people who were set free are oppressed again. What chapter 20 protected, a man's new house, his vineyard and his bride, is exactly what verse 30 takes from him.

These verses are not relished by the one who speaks them. They are spoken by Moses, who has spent forty years praying for this people. He speaks them so that they will not happen.

Who is addressed matters as much here as in the blessings. The ‘you’ is Israel as a nation in covenant with God, and the subject is the nation's life in its land over generations. The Bible itself tells when these things came. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC. Israel's own prophets and historians read those events by this chapter.

The hard question below says what the chapter must never be used for.
passages.later:
The books of Kings tell the end of the northern kingdom in this chapter's terms: “So Israel was exiled from their homeland into Assyria” (2 Kings 17:23). And of the south: “So Judah was taken into exile, away from its own land” (2 Kings 25:21).

Daniel, praying in exile, read his people's disaster by this chapter and put himself inside the confession: ‘so the oath and the curse written in the Law of Moses the servant of God has been poured out on us, because we have sinned against You’ (Daniel 9:11).

Leviticus has a chapter of the same kind, and it ends with a promise: “Yet in spite of this, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject or despise them so as to destroy them and break My covenant with them” (Leviticus 26:44).

Paul says that the curse of the law did not have the last word: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter mean that sickness, poverty or loss is God's curse on a person? And does it explain the later sufferings of the Jewish people?

No, to both. The chapter has been used in both ways, and each use has to be named and refused.

First, it is not a rule for reading any one person's life. It speaks to Israel as a nation in its land under the covenant of Sinai. It describes where a whole people's life is heading over time. The rest of the Bible will not let it be turned on an individual. Job suffers though God himself calls him ‘blameless and upright’ (Job 1:8). When Jesus was asked whose sin had made a man blind, he said, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3).

So this chapter is never God's verdict on your illness, your poverty, your childlessness or your loss. No one should be told that their illness or disability is a punishment. A person who uses these verses to tell a grieving family that they brought it on themselves is misusing them.

Second, the chapter is not a prediction or an explanation of what the Jewish people have suffered in the centuries since. For a long time some Christians read chapters like this as God's lasting curse on the Jewish people, and took the sufferings of Jews as proof. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. These are Israel's own Scriptures, in which Israel confesses its own sin, and they are followed at once by God's promise to restore his people (30:1-10). Paul, a Jew, asks, “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1). The note on Acts 2:22-28 says more.

These notes say nothing against any people, ancient or modern.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Moses spoke the curses so that they would not come. Ask whether there is a warning you have been given, in Scripture or by someone who loves you, that you have heard as an attack. And if someone has ever told you that your suffering was God's curse, set this chapter's true address against that. It was not written about you.

passages.happening:
The last part of the chapter is the darkest. It begins with a reason. “Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joy and gladness of heart in all your abundance, you will serve your enemies” (verses 47-48).

God will bring a nation from far away, swift as an eagle, ‘a nation whose language you will not understand’, with ‘no respect for the old and no pity for the young’ (verses 49-50). It will besiege every city until the walls Israel trusted have fallen (verse 52).

The siege will bring famine so terrible that people will do what no parent could imagine doing (verses 53-57).

At last the people will be torn from the land. “Then the LORD will scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other” (verse 64). There they will find no rest. ‘In the morning you will say, “If only it were evening!” and in the evening you will say, “If only it were morning!”’ (verse 67). The final verse sends them back to Egypt, to be sold as slaves, ‘but no one will buy you’ (verse 68).
passages.hearers:
The curses have come in waves, each worse than the one before. This is the last wave.

Verse 47 gives a reason that is easy to miss. The charge is not only that Israel disobeyed. It is that Israel had plenty and did not serve God ‘with joy and gladness of heart’. In this book a thankless heart in good times is where the fall begins. Chapter 8 warned of it.

A siege was the most dreaded form of war in the ancient world. An army surrounded a city and starved it. Verses 53 to 57 describe what hunger at its worst does to people, even the gentlest. The verses are hard to read, and they are meant to be. The Bible records elsewhere, with horror, that such things did happen when Samaria and Jerusalem were besieged. These notes do not dwell on them.

The nation that swoops like an eagle and speaks a language no one understands is a picture the prophets later used of Assyria and of Babylon.

The end of the chapter runs Israel's story backward. The people who became as many as the stars are left few (verse 62). The people brought out of Egypt are sent back there. The people freed from slavery offer themselves as slaves, and are not even wanted. Everything the exodus gave is taken away.

Verse 67 is one of the bleakest sentences in the Bible. It describes a life in which every hour is something to be got through.

Two things must be kept in mind by anyone who reads this far.

The chapter is not the end of the book. Chapter 30 follows, and it begins after the curse has fallen: ‘then He will restore you from captivity and have compassion on you’ (30:3). The God who speaks these warnings has already decided not to let them be the last word.

And the chapter is not about any reader's private sorrow or about the later history of the Jewish people. The hard question on verses 15 to 46 says so plainly, and it applies to every line here.
passages.later:
The book of Lamentations was written in the ruins of Jerusalem, after the siege. In the middle of it stands this: “Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!” (Lamentations 3:22-23).

This book itself promises what comes after exile: ‘then He will restore you from captivity and have compassion on you and gather you from all the nations’ (Deuteronomy 30:3).

When Jesus came near Jerusalem for the last time, he did not pronounce a curse over it. “As Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it” (Luke 19:41).
passages.asks: Verse 47 says the trouble began with plenty received without joy or thanks. Ask whether you serve God gladly in what you have now. And if you have ever lived through hours like those of verse 67, wishing the time away, remember that this chapter is followed by chapter 30, and that Jesus wept over the city.
